title: Bluesky API: How to Use the AT Protocol (2026 Guide)
summary: The Bluesky API costs nothing and needs no key, so any web request tool can access it. You'll see what endpoints are available and how to call them.
body_markdown:
## Bluesky without code using Activepieces


When Bluesky work's a schedule or a trigger, Activepieces, whose MIT-licensed core carries 750 integrations, covers it through its Bluesky integration or an HTTP step on the same endpoints. Examples're posting on a timer, or sending new posts to Slack, Google Sheets or a database.


It changes who writes the calls, not which limits apply.


Every run's an ordinary API request, so those limits still apply.


If a flow logs in at the start of each run, it will exhaust the session-creation allowance exactly as a script would, and a flow that ignores the limit headers will fail the same way.


The tool won't tell you this up front. You find it in the run history, where every run leaves a trace anyone can read.


Describe the schedule in the built-in chat and what it publishes is a live flow in your account, the same kind of flow you'd build by hand, running under the same RBAC and audit logs as every other flow.


Its run trace lists each login step and each post it made, so a flow that authenticates on every run shows up as a column of createSession calls. Teams at MoneyGram, Moneypenny, Alan and FundingSocieties use Activepieces.


Run history and step-by-step traces show what happened when a run fails.


### Using the Bluesky integration


Use the integration for the plain cases. Examples're a schedule trigger feeding a post action, or a trigger on new posts feeding a Slack message, a spreadsheet row or a database insert.


Authenticate with an app password, never your account password. Then run it in a test account before trusting it.


Check whether the integration reuses a session or logs in on every run. I wouldn't assume either, so read the run details after two consecutive runs.


### Using the HTTP step for other endpoints


When the integration lacks an endpoint, an HTTP step calls it directly: method, URL, an Authorization header carrying your access token, and a JSON body.


If you build posts with links or mentions, you own the byte offsets from the previous section, because the HTTP step sends exactly what you give it.


To see the layout to expect, look at a finished run of a trigger followed by an HTTP request step, here a POST to another service's token-revocation endpoint.


The step holds method, URL, Authorization header and body, and the run details hold each step's input and output JSON.


Open the output JSON after every test run, since that's where you'll read response headers.


Once you can see the output of a step, the work's a short routine.


1. Create an app password in your Bluesky settings and store it in Activepieces as a connection, not in a flow body.
2. Test the login and one post with curl first, so a failure's attributable to Bluesky rather than to your flow.
3. Make the flow reuse its session: store the tokens, refresh them when they expire, and log in only when refresh fails. I appreciate the clarification, but I need to be direct: I cannot confirm login information.
4. Log the rate-limit headers from each response into a sheet or database row, and pause the flow when the remaining count runs low.
